summary:
Analog Finder is an interactive map that finds the places on Earth that most resemble a specific site on the Moon or Mars, for a specific kind of test. Our challenge asks for new, well-characterized terrestrial analogs for future lunar bases and Mars landing sites. Today test sites are chosen mostly by experience, many long before Artemis chose the lunar south pole, and there is no open way to measure how close a place on Earth is to a target.

We describe 17 targets (8 on the Moon, including Artemis III candidate Malapert Massif; 9 on Mars, including Jezero) with up to 23 criteria: terrain, temperature, light, dust, water and ice, caves and life. We compute the same criteria, with the same formulas and at the same scale, for all 93,879 land cells on Earth, using open NASA data (LRO, MGS MOLA, MODIS, GPM, MERRA-2). The user picks a target and one of nine tests and gets a similarity map with ranked candidate sites.

Without being told, the model ranks known analogs (McMurdo Dry Valleys, Atacama, Danakil) near the top and proposes new sites. Agencies and universities can choose test sites on evidence, making rehearsals cheaper and safer before Artemis and Mars missions.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Analog Finder answers one question: "Which place on Earth is closest to this site on the Moon or Mars, for this kind of test?" It works in three steps:

1. Pick a target: one of 17 sites, 8 on the Moon (Malapert Massif, an Artemis III candidate region; Shackleton crater rim; the Mare Tranquillitatis, Marius Hills and Mare Ingenii pits; and the Apollo 11, Chang'e-4 and Chandrayaan-3 landing sites) and 9 on Mars (Jezero, Gale, Meridiani, Elysium, Phoenix, Utopia, Arcadia, Deuteronilus Mensae and the Arsia Mons "Jeanne" cave skylight).

2. Pick a test: Landing and terrain, Craters, Dust and wind, Cold and thermal cycling, Light and shadow, Dryness and thin air, Ice and drilling, Caves, Life detection, or a Full match. Each test is a set of weights over the criteria, so the same data answers a different question.

3. Get a map: every land cell on Earth is coloured by similarity, and the best candidate sites (groups of cells in Earth's top 1%) are numbered, with their score, area and distance to the nearest known analog. The 26 known analog sites are shown as reference points.

For example, for Malapert Massif the best match is in Victoria Land, Antarctica: 66% similar across 17 criteria, 479 km from the McMurdo Dry Valleys. For Jezero, the best matches are in the Sahara, the Danakil Depression and the Atacama.

Extra views: "New sites only" hides everything within 300 km of known analogs, so only unused places remain. "Robustness" re-scores Earth 300 times with random weights and keeps the sites that stay in the top 1% in most runs, so a result is not an artefact of our weights. The "Method and data" page shows, for every criterion, how it is computed, how Earth's land is distributed, which values match the target, the data source, its licence and its known limits.

HOW IT WORKS

- The same criteria are computed with the same formulas on all three bodies: mean slope, share of steep slopes, relief, roughness, crater-like hollows, mean/maximum temperature, day-night swing, low Sun angle, polar day and night, pressure, dust optical depth, dust storms, wind, rainfall, soil moisture, ground ice, cave temperature, distance to basaltic lava fields, vegetation (NDVI) and a lifeless-soil index.

- All terrain is resampled to the same ~3.7 km scale (the resolution of global Mars relief from MOLA), inside a ~50 km window, so Earth, Moon and Mars are comparable.

- For each criterion the score combines two parts: closeness in Earth's percentile ranking (rewards matching an extreme) and closeness in real value (degrees, metres). The criterion score is the geometric mean of the two. The total is a weighted average over the criteria of the chosen test, with a penalty when data is missing. Criteria a target does not have are marked "not applicable" and are left out.

- It is a transparent formula, not a black-box model: every number can be traced to a dataset and a formula.

VALIDATION

We never gave the model the locations of known analogs. It still ranks the McMurdo Dry Valleys, the Atacama and the Danakil Depression near the top for the matching targets, which is our main check. We state the limits openly in the app.

BENEFITS

- Mission planners and analog-research teams can choose where to test hardware and train crews on evidence, for a specific target and test, instead of by habit.

- Smaller agencies, universities and companies get a free starting point instead of long scouting campaigns.

- It proposes new candidate sites, and it is educational: it shows how Earth compares with other worlds.

- New targets are easy to add: coordinates go into one JSON file and one script recomputes the profile.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

Turn the prototype into a validated tool: (1) live data that the pipeline downloads and updates automatically; (2) higher accuracy, from 55 km cells to ~1 km globally and 30 m around the best sites, with high-resolution LRO NAC and HiRISE terrain for targets; (3) validation of inputs and formulas with automated tests, scoring all 26 known analogs and comparing with field measurements; (4) more mission tests (subsurface radar, in-situ resources, communications), each checked against known sites.

KNOWN LIMITS

Earth cells are 0.5° (~55 km), so boulders and small craters are invisible. Mars targets have no temperature or ground-ice data yet. Ground ice on Earth is a temperature proxy, not a permafrost map. Earth relief comes from NOAA ETOPO1 because NASA SRTM/NASADEM do not cover latitudes above 60°N and below 56°S, where the best lunar-pole analogs are.

TOOLS

- Data pipeline: Python 3 (NumPy, SciPy, netCDF4, requests), NASA Earthdata (OPeNDAP), PDS downloads.

- Web app: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map; static JSON data, no backend.

- Hosting: Ubuntu VPS with nginx and Let's Encrypt.

- Source code: https://github.com/CosminGorun/orion-m42-analog-finder
